title: Building an Equation from Two Points

scenes.title: Two points — can you build the whole line?
body: First find the line's rate, then its position.
scenes.narration: Suppose a line passes through two comma five and six comma thirteen. How do those two points determine one equation? Here’s the idea: two points tell us both how the line moves and where it sits. We first find the rate of change, then use either point to lock the line into position.

scenes.title: Find slope — but keep the order consistent
scenes.narration: Slope is change in y divided by change in x. So we get thirteen minus five over six minus two, which is eight over four, or two. This is where students often mix things up: if you subtract the y-values in one direction, you must subtract the x-values in that same direction. Reversing both is fine. Reversing only one changes the sign and gives the wrong slope.

scenes.title: Use one point to find b
scenes.narration: Now we know how steep the line is, but not where it crosses the y-axis. Put the slope into y equals m x plus b, and use one known point. With x equals two and y equals five, we get five equals two times two plus b. Notice why this works: the point must satisfy the equation because it lies on the line.

scenes.title: Solve for the intercept
scenes.narration: Simplify: five equals four plus b, so b equals one. The slope two tells us the line rises two units for every one unit to the right. The intercept one tells us the y-value when x is zero. Together they describe the entire line.

scenes.title: Equation: y = 2x + 1
scenes.narration: So the equation is y equals two x plus one. Quick check: two times two plus one is five, and two times six plus one is thirteen. Both original points work. The key idea is simple: two points give you the slope, and one of those points then gives you the intercept. The full lesson is available on SUMMIT. Find the complete lesson below.
